text:
The Long Way Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. The mission was Apollo 13, the third planned lunar landing. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran on his fourth spaceflight. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was making his first. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons. Swigert, a bachelor and a skilled engineer, stepped in with almost no time to spare.

The first two days went so smoothly that the networks barely bothered to broadcast the crew's television transmissions. The spacecraft was named Odyssey, and its lunar module, which would carry Lovell and Haise to the surface, was named Aquarius. The two craft were linked nose to nose and coasting toward the Moon, nearly two hundred thousand miles from home. Then, on the evening of April 13, controllers in Houston asked the crew to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, a routine step that keeps the supercold contents from stratifying.

Swigert threw the switch. A little over ninety seconds later, the crew heard a bang and felt a shudder run through the ship. Warning lights lit up. Swigert reported a problem first, and Lovell repeated it, in words that became famous: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first nobody grasped how bad it was. Voltage was dropping on the main electrical buses. Oxygen pressure in one tank read zero, and the second was falling. Out the window, Lovell saw gas streaming into space. The explosion of oxygen tank number two had crippled the service module, the section that supplied power, water and breathable air. The command module's fuel cells, which generated electricity by combining oxygen and hydrogen, were starving. Within hours the crew would be left with only the batteries meant for reentry.

Investigators later traced the cause to a chain of small errors that began years earlier. The tank had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory. During a ground test before launch, its heaters ran far too long and burned away the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside. Nobody knew. When Swigert activated the stirring fans in flight, bare wires sparked inside a tank full of pure oxygen, and the tank failed.

The landing was impossible now. The only question was whether the men could be brought home alive. Gene Kranz, the flight director, rallied his teams and set them to work. The solution was as strange as the problem. Aquarius, built to keep two men alive for about two days on the lunar surface, would become a lifeboat for three men for four days. Lovell, Haise and Swigert crowded into the cramped lunar module and shut down Odyssey completely to save its precious batteries.

The route home was its own puzzle. The spacecraft was on a path that would swing around the Moon and then return toward Earth, but it would miss the planet by a wide margin. A burn of the lunar module's descent engine was needed to correct the course. Controllers also planned a second, longer burn after the ship rounded the far side of the Moon, to speed up the return and bring the splashdown into daylight in the Pacific, where recovery ships waited. Lovell flew the first burn by hand, with Mission Control feeding him numbers. The crew passed behind the Moon, out of radio contact, and looked down on a landscape they had come so close to touching. Haise later said that nobody much felt like admiring the view.

Then came the problem of the air. Carbon dioxide was building up inside the lunar module, which carried only enough lithium hydroxide canisters for two men over a short stay. Odyssey had plenty of canisters, but they were square, and the lunar module's receptacles were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the very items the crew had aboard, which included plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual cover, a sock, hoses and duct tape. They devised an adapter and read the instructions up to space. The crew built it, and the carbon dioxide readings fell. It remains one of the most celebrated improvisations in the history of spaceflight.

Meanwhile, the cold set in. With almost everything switched off, the cabin temperature sank to near freezing, and moisture condensed on the walls. The men slept little, wore whatever extra clothing they had, and rationed water to a few ounces a day. Haise developed a fever and a urinary infection. Lovell, Haise and Swigert were thirsty, exhausted and chilled, yet they continued to perform their tasks with discipline.

Back in Houston, the real work was devising a way to restart Odyssey. A normal power-up sequence took hours and drew far more energy than the batteries could give. Mattingly, who had been bumped from the flight and never did get the measles, spent long hours in a simulator with engineers writing a new procedure that powered up systems one at a time in an order that stretched every amp hour. When the crew performed it near the end of the flight, they had to use it without any practice. It worked.

Several smaller dangers still loomed. A late course correction had to be made, and with the ship's guidance systems off, the crew aligned the spacecraft by sighting the Earth's day and night boundary, using the sunlit edge of the planet as a reference. Then, hours before reentry, they jettisoned the service module and saw, for the first time, what the explosion had done. A whole panel of its outer skin was gone, and equipment hung out of the gap. Lovell described it as a mess. It was a shock, and it raised new fears about whether the heat shield on the command module might also be damaged.

Last, they discarded Aquarius, which had saved their lives, and it burned up in the atmosphere. On April 17, Odyssey plunged into the atmosphere alone. Reentry always brings a blackout in radio contact, normally lasting about three minutes. This time the silence seemed endless. Controllers sat watching the clock and the empty channel, and the minutes ticked past what the plan had allowed. Then Swigert's voice came through, and soon afterward three parachutes blossomed in the sky.

Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, a little under six days after launch. The crew was thinner, dehydrated and worn, but unharmed. Millions around the world had followed their ordeal on radio and television, and the relief was widespread.

The accident forced NASA to redesign the oxygen tanks and tighten safety practices before flights resumed. Apollo went on to land astronauts on the Moon again, but the flight of Apollo 13 is remembered for a different kind of triumph. It was a mission that failed in its original goal and succeeded at something harder, which was bringing three men home through a series of cascading failures by careful thinking, courage and cooperation between the people in space and the thousands on the ground. Lovell never walked on the Moon, but he is remembered for the voyage home.
